function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run inside a script) to finish the whole pipeline.  
I’ll also include the exact content for the three files you asked for – Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow – so you only need to paste them into the appropriate locations.

> ⚠️ **Important:** I don’t have permission to execute `git` or `docker` commands from here, so this is *instructions* rather than an automated run.  
> Make sure you’re logged into the machine that has access to the remote repo (`ssh -T git@github.com`) before running the commands below.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1.1 Go to the folder where you want the repo
cd ~/projects   # change as needed

# 1.2 Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you already have the repo locally, just `cd` into it.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output might look like:

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

From this we know:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `src/index.js` | Main entry point |
| `package.json` | Node dependencies + start script |
| `README.md` | Project description |

---

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use official lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY src ./src

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small and fast.  
> * We install only production deps (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * The app listens on port `3000` (adjust if your app uses another port).  

---

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                 # exposed externally
    targetPort: 3000         # matches containerPort above
```

> **Notes**  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you’ll push to.  
> * If you’re not using a cloud provider that supports `LoadBalancer`, switch to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.

---

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # required for pushing to GHCR

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        push: true
```

> **What this does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image using the Dockerfile we created.  
> * Tags it as `ghcr.io/<owner>/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * Pushes it to GitHub Packages (GHCR).  

Make sure the repo’s **Settings → Secrets → Actions** has a secret named `GITHUB_TOKEN` (this is automatically available in workflows; no extra secret needed unless you use a custom token).

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

If you want to stage everything that changed (including potential updates to existing files), you can simply run:

```bash
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger, building and publishing the Docker image.

---

## Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, verify the image exists:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

And test the deployment locally (optional):

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome
```

That’s it! You now have a fully automated CI/CD pipeline that builds a Docker image on every push to `main`, stores it in GHCR, and provides Kubernetes manifests ready for deployment.
